name: Central Place Theory
statement: Settlements form a hierarchy of central places whose hexagonal market areas are set by each good's threshold demand and maximum travel range.
statementAccent: threshold demand and maximum travel range
meaning: Central place theory explains why some settlements are large, rare, and widely spaced — offering many high-order goods — while others are small, common, and close together, offering only frequently bought low-order goods. Every good or service has a "threshold," the minimum demand needed to support it, and a "range," the farthest distance people will travel to obtain it; together these determine the size and spacing of market areas.
mechanism: On a uniform plain with evenly distributed population and purchasing power, competing central places' circular market areas pack together and, to avoid gaps or overlap, tessellate into hexagons. Christaller proposed three ideal networks depending on which principle dominates: a k=3 marketing-optimizing hierarchy, a k=4 transport-optimizing hierarchy, and a k=7 administrative-optimizing hierarchy, each nesting lower-order centers within the market areas of higher-order ones.

examples.text: Christaller developed and tested the theory on the settlement pattern of southern Germany in his 1933 book Die zentralen Orte in Süddeutschland (Central Places in Southern Germany).
Later empirical tests found the Midwestern United States, particularly Iowa and Wisconsin, came closest among studied regions to matching Christaller's idealized hexagonal settlement pattern.
German economist August Lösch generalized the theory in The Spatial Organization of the Economy (1940), deriving Christaller's three k-value systems from a triangular-hexagonal lattice of farms.

whyItMatters: It remains a core framework in urban and regional geography for explaining settlement size hierarchies, retail location, and service-provision planning, and it influenced real urban and regional planning policy in the 20th century.
limits: The theory assumes a flat, uniform plain with even population density, purchasing power, and transport cost in all directions. It fits agricultural service-center regions better than industrial or highly urbanized ones, and it is largely static, ignoring history, topography, and changing technology.
misreadings: It is sometimes mistaken for a theory of city-size distribution generally, like rank-size rules, rather than specifically a theory of market-area geometry and service-center hierarchy.
origin: Proposed by the German geographer Walter Christaller in Die zentralen Orte in Süddeutschland (1933), his doctoral work, from an analysis of the towns of southern Germany. Christaller asked why settlements come in a hierarchy of sizes rather than a jumble, and answered it with the threshold demand each good needs and the distance a shopper will travel for it — producing the nested hexagonal market areas the theory is remembered for.

sources.text: Britannica's entry noting Walter Christaller introduced central-place theory in Central Places in Southern Germany (1933) — supports the origin, year, and threshold/range mechanism.
Wikipedia's account of central place theory, its hexagonal market areas, and the k=3, k=4, and k=7 variants — supports the hierarchy mechanism and examples.
